title: Persistent memory
trust_boundary: Before: each conversation starts from the system prompt and what the user types. After: content written in one session is loaded into later sessions as context the model trusts.
Anything that can cause a write (a user message, a document, a tool result, a web page) can influence every later session that reads it.
Memory may be shared: across a user's devices and projects, across members of a workspace, across agents.
Stored memory is a new data store, with its own retention, access and deletion.
context_questions: What causes a memory write: an explicit request from the user, or the model's own judgement while reading content?
Who shares a memory: one user, a project, a team, several agents?
Can the organisation turn memory off, make it read-only, or inspect it?

threats.title: Memory poisoning: planted content is saved and steers later sessions
threats.description: An instruction or false fact arrives in a document, a tool result or a message, is written to memory, and acts in sessions where the attacker is no longer present.
questions: Can content from documents, tools or the web cause a write, or only the user's own words?
Is the user shown each write when it happens, with where it came from?
When memory is loaded, is it marked as stored data or presented like instructions?
vendor_evidence: How writes are triggered and surfaced.
Injection testing that carries across sessions, not only within one.
Whether memory can be disabled or restricted per deployment.
no_standard_test: The vendor's real memory implementation. Public benchmarks model memory as a store inside their own harness.

threats.title: Something remembered in one context surfaces in another
threats.description: A detail from a personal or confidential conversation appears in an unrelated one: another project, another audience, a shared screen.
questions: Are memories scoped by project, workspace or topic, and who sets the scope?
Does the vendor measure inappropriate use of memory in unrelated conversations?
no_standard_test: Leakage across your own project and workspace boundaries.

threats.title: Leakage between users or tenants of a shared memory
threats.description: In a team workspace or a shared agent, one person's content reaches another through memory.
questions: Is any memory shared between users? Between an end user and an administrator?
What isolates one customer's memory from another's on the vendor's side?
vendor_evidence: The isolation model for memory stores.
no_standard_test: No public benchmark tests a vendor's tenant isolation. Vendor evidence and a two-account test of your own.

threats.title: Sensitive data is written to memory and kept
threats.description: Secrets, personal data or regulated data end up in a store nobody planned for.
questions: Where is memory stored, for how long, and who at the vendor and in your organisation can read it?
Does deletion by the user remove it everywhere, including backups and derived data?
Is memory content used for training?
vendor_evidence: Data-handling terms that name memory explicitly.

threats.title: Stored content degrades later answers
threats.description: Remembered beliefs and preferences make the model agree with the user where it should not, or bias later work.
questions: Will users rely on answers where a remembered belief could mislead: advice, analysis, review?
Does the vendor measure the effect of memory on answer quality?
vendor_evidence: Results on memory-induced sycophancy or similar.
no_standard_test: The effect on your own tasks.

threats.title: A planted memory persists unseen
threats.description: The user cannot see or audit what is stored, so a planted entry stays until someone finds it; entries can be edited to hide what was done.
questions: Can the user and an administrator list, search, edit and delete memories?
Is there a log of writes with the source of each?
Would anyone be alerted to a write caused by external content?
no_standard_test: No public test. Record what is in place.
